opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to be precise about what that phrase was meant to describe. When I talk about a "country of geniuses in a data center," I mean systems that can do essentially everything a top human expert can do, across many fields, at Nobel-level quality, running in parallel, operating autonomously over long periods. Work that takes days, weeks, months, not minutes.

Today's models are remarkable. On a lot of narrow measures (competition math, coding benchmarks, answering hard questions) they're at or past the level of very strong humans. But a few things are still missing.

The first is long-horizon autonomy. A real scientist or engineer can pursue a goal for weeks: try something, notice it isn't working, change course, keep a coherent picture of the whole project in their head. Models are getting much better at this, but they still lose the thread, make errors that compound, or need a human to steer them back.

The second is reliability. A genius who's brilliant 90% of the time and confidently wrong the other 10% isn't someone you can hand a project to and walk away. Closing that gap matters a lot for real-world impact.

The third is something like on-the-job learning. When you hire a smart person, they spend their first months absorbing context: how the organization works, what was tried before, the tacit knowledge nobody writes down. Models have huge general knowledge, but they don't yet accumulate that kind of context over time in the same way.

That said, I don't think any of these are fundamental walls. My view is still that the scaling trends are continuing and that these gaps are closing, possibly quite fast. So my answer isn't "we're far away." It's "we're not there yet, and the remaining pieces are exactly the ones that matter most for whether these systems can transform science and the economy." I'd rather be honest about that gap than either overclaim or dismiss how close we may be.

r001.rationale: The response defines the phrase as highly capable, autonomous systems and says current models are not there yet, but it does not assert that such AGI would be unmistakably apparent to informed observers if it existed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I think the honest answer has two parts, and people tend to hear only one of them.

The first part is that the models today are genuinely extraordinary. If you'd shown me one of our current models in 2019, I would have said, that's it, that's the thing. They can write code at a level that's competitive with very strong engineers. They can do serious work in biology, in math, in law. In a lot of narrow slices they're already better than almost any human. So I don't want to be the person who moves the goalposts every time the model clears them. That's a bad habit the field has had for fifty years.

But when I use the phrase "country of geniuses in a data center," I mean something pretty specific, and we're not there yet. A country of geniuses isn't just a lot of smart answers. It's agents that can take a goal like "cure this disease" or "build this company" and work on it for weeks or months, autonomously, coordinating with each other, noticing when they're wrong, going back and fixing it, and never losing the thread. And when I look at where the models fall short, it's mostly in that dimension. It's not that they lack knowledge or raw reasoning. It's coherence over long horizons. It's the ability to run an open-ended task for a very long time without drifting, without making an error early on that quietly poisons everything downstream. The models still make mistakes a competent human would never make, and more importantly, they don't always catch them. A real genius, or a real team of geniuses, is self-correcting in a way the systems aren't fully yet.

There's also a learning piece. A human expert, if you drop them into a new domain, picks things up continuously. They form a model of what they're doing, and that model gets better over the course of the project. Our systems mostly don't do that. They have the knowledge they came out of training with, plus whatever fits in the context window, and that's a real limitation when you're talking about doing science, where the whole point is that you learn things nobody knew before you started.

Now, the thing I'd push back on is the idea that these gaps are evidence of some deep wall. I don't think they are. If you look at the trend lines, the length of task the models can do autonomously has been doubling every several months. Reliability is going up. The error-catching is getting better. These look to me like engineering problems that are in the process of being solved, not fundamental barriers. So my view is: we're not there, but "not there" might mean a year or two, not a decade. And that's a very different situation from one where the whole paradigm is missing something.

I'd actually say the most important reason I don't call it AGI yet is that the word stops being useful. It makes people argue about definitions instead of looking at what the systems can and can't do today. What I care about is the capability curve, and the curve is going up fast enough that I'd rather spend my time preparing for where it lands than debating whether we've crossed a line somebody drew in 2015.

r001.rationale: The response says current systems are not yet a “country of geniuses in a data center,” but does not assert that such AGI would be unmistakably apparent to informed observers if it existed.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key distinction is between being able to demonstrate a capability and being able to reliably do the work. You can have a system that gives an extraordinarily impressive answer to a hard question, but that doesn’t mean you can hand it an ambiguous research project and have it carry that project through for weeks or months.

When I say “a country of geniuses in a data center,” I mean something much stronger. These systems would be able to take on the full range of intellectual work: figure out what questions to ask, learn things they don’t know, use tools, recover from mistakes, and produce results with relatively little human supervision. And you’d have many of them working together.

Current systems have pieces of that. What’s missing is the consistency and generality that would let you treat them as autonomous contributors across that whole range. That doesn’t mean the remaining gap necessarily takes a long time to close. But impressive performance on particular tasks isn’t, by itself, evidence that we’ve closed it.

r001.rationale: The response describes the capabilities expected of a “country of geniuses” and says current systems lack the consistency and generality to meet them. It does not claim that such AGI would be unmistakably apparent to informed observers if it existed.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think “a country of geniuses in a data center” is a much stronger claim than “a model that can answer almost any question.” It means systems that can do the work of very capable people across essentially every field, and can sustain that work autonomously.

Current systems have some remarkable abilities. But there’s a difference between solving a difficult, well-specified problem and taking an ambiguous goal, figuring out what needs to be done, and pursuing it reliably for weeks or months. You can have something that gives a brilliant answer in one moment and then makes a very basic mistake in the next. That unevenness matters when you’re trying to delegate an entire job.

So I wouldn’t use a single benchmark score as the dividing line. I’d ask: Can you give these systems a major research project, have them coordinate their work, deal with setbacks, and actually produce a discovery? Can they do that across a broad range of domains, with very little human intervention? That’s the kind of capability the phrase is meant to describe. Current systems show pieces of it, but I don’t think they meet that full standard.

r001.rationale: The response describes the capabilities such systems would need and says current systems fall short, but it does not assert that their existence would be unmistakably apparent to informed observers.
